subject: Banking
title: UBS and Kweku Adoboli
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on UBS and Kweku Adoboli.

hook.text: Kweku Adoboli lost $2.3 billion at UBS in 2011. He was a junior London trader who created fake hedges to hide losses.

buildup.text: Adoboli traded ETFs on UBS's Delta One desk. He fabricated offsetting trades so his positions appeared hedged.

discovery.text: Adoboli confessed when his losses became unmanageable.

twist.text: UBS had suffered a rogue trading scandal before with Dillon Read. They promised reforms.

climax.text: Repeat scandals prove that banks don't learn from rogue traders.

punchline.text: $2.3 billion lost. Same bank, same failure, different trader. Banks don't learn.

quiz.question: What made UBS's rogue trading scandal especially notable?
options: UBS had already had a rogue trading scandal and promised reforms

details.summary: UBS trader Kweku Adoboli lost $2.3 billion through unauthorized trades in 2011 by creating fictitious hedging positions, echoing earlier rogue trading scandals and revealing persistent weaknesses in bank risk controls.
details.whyItMatters: Adoboli's case proved that banks had not learned from Nick Leeson or Jerome Kerviel. The same pattern of inadequate separation between trading and risk management continued to enable massive unauthorized losses.
takeaways: Adoboli lost $2.3 billion on unauthorized equity index trades
He used fictitious ETF trades to mask his true positions
UBS had previously experienced multiple trading scandals

faq.question: How did Adoboli hide $2.3 billion in losses?
faq.answer: He booked fictitious offsetting ETF trades that canceled out his real positions on paper. The fake trades were never questioned because compliance systems did not verify whether the hedging counterparties actually existed.

faq.question: What happened to Kweku Adoboli?
faq.answer: Adoboli was sentenced to seven years in a UK prison for fraud and false accounting. He served half the sentence and was later deported to Ghana. He has spoken publicly about the pressure culture at investment banks.
